analysis.one_liner: Lets merchants collectively negotiate the fees they pay to accept credit and debit cards.
analysis.headline: Introduced by one Democrat and one Republican, the bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on June 5, 2008 and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Credit and debit card networks like Visa and MasterCard set the fees merchants must pay to accept their cards, and merchants cannot negotiate individually. This bill would let merchants band together to negotiate those fees without breaking antitrust laws, and if negotiations failed, a panel of three government-appointed judges would set the fee schedule based on what a competitive market would produce. Merchants negotiate with the card companies; consumers pay those fees indirectly in the price of goods.
analysis.who_benefits: Merchants — especially small businesses that have no bargaining power against Visa and MasterCard — would gain if the bill passed, because the fees they pay on every card transaction would be set through negotiation or by a judge using competitive-market standards rather than unilaterally by the card networks [S2][S3]. Ordinary consumers would benefit indirectly, since merchants pass interchange fees on in the prices of goods and services [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Merchants, especially small businesses, and shoppers

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes providers of a payment system and merchants to jointly negotiate the fees and terms for access to that system, with limited antitrust immunity so merchants can bargain as a group [S2].

If no voluntary agreement is reached, a panel of three Electronic Payment System Judges appointed by the Justice Department's Antitrust Division and the FTC would set the fee schedule for two-year periods, selecting between the two sides' final offers based on what fees would look like in a perfectly competitive market [S2].
The bill requires the 10 largest card issuers, acquirers, and merchants to disclose their itemized costs, and makes all fee determinations and negotiated agreements publicly available [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Card networks like Visa and MasterCard and the banks that issue their cards would bear the cost if the bill passed, since interchange fees are a large revenue stream and the bill would replace unilateral fee-setting with negotiation or judicially set rates pegged to competitive-market costs [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Card issuers could shift lost interchange revenue onto cardholders through higher annual fees, higher interest rates, or reduced rewards programs, so some of the savings to merchants could come at cardholders' expense [S2].

The bill substitutes government-adjudicated rates for market prices, a form of regulated pricing that critics of rate-setting argue can misjudge costs and reduce investment in the payment system; the bill also builds a permanent three-judge adjudicatory panel and a new fee-setting bureaucracy [S3].

Merchants could instead sign voluntary agreements with the card companies, and those agreements would override the judges' rates, leaving open the possibility that large merchants cut favorable side deals while smaller ones remain bound by the judges' schedule [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large in aggregate: interchange fees are charged on nearly every card purchase in the country and are embedded in consumer prices, and the bill attacks them at their source by giving merchants collective bargaining power backed by a competitive-market standard [S2][S3]. The main honest costs are that issuers may recover some of the loss from cardholders through fees and reduced rewards, and that the bill creates a novel rate-setting tribunal rather than relying on market competition; but given that the market is dominated by two networks that set take-it-or-leave-it rates, the market-competition alternative the bill relies on does not exist today. On balance the bill is designed to move money from payment networks and issuers to merchants and, through prices, to consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 110th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the bill on June 5, 2008 with one Republican cosponsor [S1][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
The bill received no further action of any kind before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Card networks and the banks that issue their cards are better off because the bill died: they continued to set interchange fees unilaterally, with no negotiation, no judicial review, and no public cost disclosure, while merchants and shoppers kept paying the fees.

sides.party_line_note: Only two senators sponsored the bill — one Democrat and one Republican — and no votes were ever held, so its partisan shape cannot be measured from the record [S4].

industries.note: The bill strips the networks of their power to unilaterally set the fees merchants must pay to accept their cards, replacing it with collective negotiation and a judge-set competitive rate. Those fees are baked into the prices shoppers pay, so the networks' interest runs against merchants and consumers.

Interchange fees collected from merchants are a major revenue source for banks that issue Visa and MasterCard branded cards. Lower, competitively set fees would shrink that revenue, and issuers could try to recover it from cardholders through fees and reduced rewards.

Merchants pay a fee on every card transaction and currently have no individual bargaining power over the rate. Lower swipe fees reduce their cost of doing business, and retailers typically pass some of that savings to customers through prices.
